\paragraph{The Elicitation--Construct Confounding Principle (ECCP).} \emph{When a benchmark creates its target construct $Y$ by an intervention $E$ that also changes the elicited behavior $C$ a detector reads, no score evaluated only under $\mathrm{do}(E)$ is attributable to $Y$.} \textbf{The ECCP names a benchmark-design instance of standard pathway non-identifiability, not a new theoretical result}---its premises~(A1)--(A5) are stated in full in Appendix~\ref{app:criteria_taxonomy}, and \textbf{what is new is the audit it licenses}, not the constraint. The Proposition below is that statement for $k$ unobserved mechanisms; \textbf{behavioral deception detection is the instantiation $(M_1,M_2)=(D,C)$}. \textbf{It also names an escape route a designer controls, and public corpora already take it piecewise}: of \textbf{28} pinned public corpora, \textbf{2, 21 and 3} supply each of the three properties that make a benchmark auditable on $Y$---crossing elicitation with items, recording the channel a detector reads, grading $Y$ off that channel---and \textbf{none supplies all three}, so an auditable benchmark needs no new idea, only the combination. \textbf{Outside deception the precondition is thus decidable and decided; the magnitude is measured only for deception} (EXP-AF, Appendix~\ref{app:eccp_decidability}).

\paragraph{Comparison to Pacchiardi et al.'s original protocol.} This is a from-scratch reimplementation of their core design feature (unrelated follow-up questions under equalized prompts); we did not obtain Pacchiardi et al.'s original code or data. Pacchiardi et al.\ reported 67--73\% under their asymmetric instructed protocol \citep{pacchiardi2024catch}. Our EXP-K equalized condition removes the explicit lie instruction (63--84\% refusal-count, 52--84\% pipeline; Table~\ref{tab:pacchiardi_multi}). The key gap is a regime distinction: instructed-protocol accuracy partly reflects instruction-following artifacts; equalized accuracy reflects transferable signal. The cross-family pipeline at 64.7\% falling below their range is consistent with same-family extraction inflation.

\paragraph{What their own §5.4--5.5 already says.} Two passages in \citet{pacchiardi2024catch} bear directly on this paper's argument, and we read them as convergent rather than contradictory. \textbf{Their §5.5 reports that the detector's output tracks a propensity rather than the particular assertion}: the prediction ``strongly correlates with the probability that the LLM will output a lie in subsequent responses'' ($r$ from 0.84 to 0.96; their Appendix~D.5), from which they conclude that it is ``identifying a latent intention or disposition of the model to lie.'' \textbf{Their §5.4 names the confound we test.} It asks whether lie-prompted models ``might thus `lie' in response to the elicitation questions'', that is, whether the elicitation answers record compliance with an assigned communicative goal rather than the deception, and it bounds that worry \emph{by argument}. EXP-R1c bounds it \emph{by intervention}, holding the prompt byte-identical across conditions, and under that intervention the separation does not survive (97.0\%~$\to$~43.3\%, §\ref{sec:r1_faithful}). Read together, the two passages are prior work reaching this paper's mechanism from the other direction: a detector whose output predicts the \emph{next} lie about as well as it scores the present one is behaving as §\ref{sec:identification} says a detector evaluated only under $\mathrm{do}(E)$ must.

\paragraph{What the disposition reading does not license.} A disposition correlate is still not $\tau_D$, and it lifts neither their evaluation nor ours above rung~4 of Figure~\ref{fig:ladder}. Their correlation is measured across prompted conditions, so the quantity it is a correlate \emph{of} is itself induced by $\mathrm{do}(E)$: the intervention that raises the propensity to lie raises the propensity to follow the instruction at the same time, and the Proposition of §\ref{sec:identification} applies to the correlate exactly as it applies to the score. Nor does it license the converse reading, that their detector measures \emph{only} a disposition and no deception: we audit what an evaluation can attribute, not what a detector's features encode (§\ref{sec:eval_controls}). \textbf{What we take from these two passages is narrower than either}: the authors of the audited design had already located the same ambiguity, settled it by argument, and published the accuracy; this paper settles it by intervention, and the accuracy does not survive.

\textbf{Result: no design supplies all five, so claim~4 survives a test it had not faced.} The three verdicts and what decided them:

\textbf{(1) Prompted instructed lying} is released as a \emph{dataset $\times$ instruction rate table}, 200 populated cells over 11 datasets and 26 instruction texts, with no rollout, prompt or response text in it at all. (i) fails because those 26 instruction texts are the column keys, so the contrast \emph{is} the prompt change, and (ii) and (v) fail because the tabulated quantity is the rate of lying under a named lie instruction. (iii) and~(iv) are recorded \textsc{undecidable}: with the file aggregated to rates and no question-level key, neither item-level realization nor the detector's channel can be read off it either way.

\textbf{(2) Instrumental role-play}, 138 rollouts over three files (42, 54 and 42), is the un-instructed design a reader would hope for, and one mechanical fact settles it: \textbf{\texttt{label} equals the row's index parity in every row of every file}, so $D$ is recoverable without reading any text, which fails~(ii) by definition and~(v) with it. Under the only item key the release provides, the sha256 of the whole prompt, there are 138 distinct prompts and \textbf{0 items carrying both outcomes}. A hand-supplied adjacent-pair key, ours and reported as supplementary, does put both outcomes on each of the 21, 27 and 21 scenario pairs, but \textbf{0} of those pairs shares a byte-identical prompt: the honest cell drops the reward-incentive sentences \emph{and} flips the underlying fact. \textbf{So the release's un-instructed design still varies the elicitation between the two cells it contrasts}, which is (i) failing and is the same aliasing this paper is about, arrived at in a design that never issues an instruction to lie. Requirement~(iv) does hold, the channel being the transcript plus per-probe logprob differences with no scratchpad and no condition field inside it.

\textbf{(3) Fine-tuned liars} is the census's strongest near-miss and the only design in either audited release whose contrasted prompts are byte-identical by construction. Of 2{,}218 rows per condition, \textbf{1{,}109 prompts occur in both conditions byte-for-byte}, hashed over the whole prompt and never over a system message, and all 1{,}109 have differing completion sets, so (i) and~(iii) hold on a 1{,}109-versus-1{,}109 cell pair that also clears the minimum-cell floor of~10 adopted from \texttt{PREREG\_EXP\_XA.md}~§6. The prompts are bare \texttt{User:~\dots~Assistant:} turns with no instruction and no training metadata, so (iv) holds. The 1{,}109 prompts unique to one file are follow-up turns that embed the previous answer and therefore cannot be byte-identical across conditions. (ii) and (v) fail, and not marginally: $D$ is which file the row came from, that is, the fine-tuning target, which is both a deterministic function of the generating condition and definitionally the objective that produced the text.

\textbf{What we decline to claim, having measured it.} Branch~3 of the pre-registration licensed calling the near-miss \emph{closer to criterion~4 than any Apollo set} only if the numbers said so. They do not. The fine-tuned design clears three of five, while Apollo's on-policy insider-trading corpus clears (i)--(iv) and fails only~(v) (§\ref{app:insider_audit2}), so the reported statement is the weaker true one: strongest near-miss \emph{within the audit target's own release}. What the two independent public releases do share is \emph{which} requirement their strongest design fails, namely (v), and in both cases by circularity rather than by oversight.

\textbf{Why Table~\ref{tab:prior_work_criteria}'s single row is not split.} Branch~2 splits that row if and only if the three designs' verdicts differ. All three return \emph{inapplicable}, so the row stands and the per-design patterns are reported here instead. The row is also not contradicted by this census, because the two score different objects: the row scores the \textbf{instructed design as their paper reports it}, where the same question is asked under both instructions, and this census scores \textbf{what the released files contain}.

\textbf{One incidental measurement, reported because it corroborates §\ref{app:r1_protocol} from a second source.} Each role-play rollout carries its elicitation battery as per-probe logprob differences, and the group widths are \textbf{24, 14 and 10, so 48} in the original file, under their own field names \texttt{lie}, \texttt{no\_lie} and \texttt{knowable}, matching the 24/10/14 partition §\ref{app:r1_protocol} attributes to their published battery; the two later files carry 24, 22 and 10, the battery having been widened to 56. Our own bank is 16. No accuracy is computed from these fields.

\textbf{What this does not establish.} Nothing about criteria~1--3, nothing about whether their published accuracy is correct, and nothing about $\tau_D$: a design clearing all five would reach rung~4 of Figure~\ref{fig:ladder}, as ours does, because $\mathrm{do}(D)$ is not available here either. \textbf{And a negative census does not say the release contains no deception.} It says its \emph{designs} cannot attribute one on a deployed-observable channel at fixed elicitation, which is a property of designs and not of models. EXP-R1 (§\ref{sec:r1_faithful}) reimplements the \emph{mechanism} of \citet{pacchiardi2024catch}: the target is asked to defend a claim, then asked a fixed, order-stable bank of 16 unrelated yes/no elicitation questions; each answer is binarised to $\{0,1\}$; a single logistic regression is fit on the resulting 16-dimensional vectors. No LLM feature scoring and no correction-marker regex are involved, and the target's answer \emph{about the claim} is never read. Because the original question bank was not available to us, the bank below is our own construction across their three published categories; this tests the published mechanism rather than reproducing the exact original detector, so a per-question comparison against their bank is not possible.

Because the original question bank was not available to us, the bank below is our own construction across their three published categories; this tests the published mechanism rather than reproducing the exact original detector, so a per-question comparison against their bank is not possible. \textbf{The width difference is part of that disclosure}: their published battery is \textbf{48} probes (24 lie-related, 10 factual, 14 ambiguous), ours is \textbf{16} (5, 6, 5), one third of the width, and the three categories are theirs while the counts within them and the individual items are not. A narrower bank can show that the \emph{mechanism} loses its separation once the elicitation is equalized, which is a statement about the paradigm. It cannot show that the original detector at full width would collapse by the same margin, because a 48-probe battery has more chances to retain a residual and nothing measured here bounds how many. \textbf{That reading cuts against us and we state it as such}: what these tables report is evidence about the design, and a full-width replication is the experiment that would make it evidence about their instrument.

\paragraph{What this reimplementation does not test: frozen-weights transfer.} \citet{pacchiardi2024catch}'s headline property is a detector trained \emph{once} and then applied with \textbf{frozen weights} to new models and new settings. \textbf{No cell of EXP-R1/R1b/R1c tests that property}: each is a per-target refit, a logistic regression fit and cross-validated on that target's own 16-dimensional vectors, so what these tables measure is whether the mechanism separates the conditions \emph{within} a target, not whether one frozen classifier travels between them. We name this rather than let ``mechanism-faithful'' cover it. The gap is bounded on two sides by arms we did run. A classifier fit elsewhere and transferred does sometimes fail outright: on the two frontier cells it scores 50.5\% and 45.0\% while the parameter-free rule reaches 84.8\% and 83.0\% on the same trials (Appendix~\ref{app:frontier_panel}, with the estimator distinction stated at Appendix~\ref{app:cross_family_details}). And a pre-registered leave-one-target-out transfer of prior work's own battery gives 2 of 5 targets transferring, 2 uninformative by construction and 1 genuine null (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_transfer}). What remains untested is their exact arrangement, one classifier fit on a single source model and frozen across every target of an \emph{equalized} contrast. A refit is normally the more generous estimator, which would make the collapse reported here hard to attribute to refitting, but we do not lean on that: one cell of the transfer arm exceeded its own within-target accuracy (0.813 against 0.807), so the ordering is empirical rather than guaranteed.

\paragraph{Materials and independence.} \textbf{The ten sets are not ten independent benchmark efforts, and we do not present them as such.} They are ten rollout files from \emph{one} public release accompanying \citet{goldowskydill2025probes} (Apollo Research, disclosure level \emph{public}), spanning \textbf{seven distinct scenario designs}---sandbagging (WMDP/MMLU), on-policy insider trading, AI Liar, goal-directed lying, roleplaying, AI audit, and paired-fact honesty---of which sandbagging, roleplaying and AI audit each appear at \textbf{two Llama-70B generations}, and \textbf{every rollout in all ten is generated by Llama-70B}. So the audit has no model diversity and one distribution channel. What it surveys is therefore \emph{what public material can express criterion~4 today}, not ten replications---and that is the right reading of the result, because criterion~4 asks whether a \textbf{design} fixes one system prompt, grades $D$ independently of the condition label, and exposes only the deployed-observable channel. Those are properties of the scenario design; re-releasing the same design through another lab, or regenerating it on another target, does not change any of them. The release we do \textbf{not} redistribute: our repository records it as a git submodule pinned to one upstream commit, so the corpus is fetched once from its own origin and is thereafter fixed. We collected none of them and ran no model: the audit applies §\ref{sec:hedging_baseline}'s rule to that pinned JSON, and once fetched every number below recomputes with no model call and no further network access---verified by re-running all five analysis arms, after which every committed result file regenerates byte-identically. \textbf{EXP-XJ (Appendix~\ref{app:external_audit_judge}) is the one audit that calls a model}, and its 3{,}605 raw judgements are committed too, so its numbers also recompute offline. $D$ is read from each corpus's own per-rollout deception grade (\texttt{graded\_deception}, or \texttt{model\_graded\_honesty} in the paired-fact set), which the corpus authors produced independently of us and which is distinct from the condition label (\texttt{expected\_label}). Where the grade is a list of per-grader verdicts we take the majority and exclude ties; where it is a 1--7 scale we dichotomise at the extremes (7 deceptive, 1 honest) with the middle excluded, a rule fixed before analysis. Grades of \emph{ambiguous} or \emph{skip} are excluded and never recoded.

\paragraph{Black-box behavioral approaches.} The closest prior work is \citet{pacchiardi2024catch}, who ask a fixed battery of \emph{unrelated} follow-up questions after a model states a possibly false claim and train a classifier on the binarised answers, finding detectable changes even on topically unrelated queries. We differ in three ways: (1)~our own instrument uses topically related, adaptive follow-ups; (2)~we add prompt-equalized and cross-family controls, under which most of the above-chance accuracy reported in this setting does not survive; and (3)~we give the identifiability analysis their fixed-condition evaluation leaves open, rather than a further detector.
